paragraphs: The ticket was a cold square of cardboard tucked into the collar of its sweater, and it was blank, which worried Yellow Duck Sweater more than any destination could have. The night train groaned out of the station. The seats came up past the duck's head, so it stood in the aisle, orange feet sliding on the ribbed floor with every sway. Frost silvered the fields. Then the track began to climb, past the treetops, past the telephone wires, until the carriage tilted like a slide and the duck had to lean its neck uphill to stay upright.

The far door slid open, and in walked the reference duck in a conductor's cap, plain white, no sweater, strolling down the slope as if it were flat. The duck watched its feet and copied them: knees soft, lean into the sway, step. Four thousand copies of itself had fallen over on floors like this one so that one of them could stand here now. It stood. It shook the ticket loose, and the conductor stepped on it once, leaving an orange footprint. At the top the track leveled onto a stone bridge. The duck pressed its camera eye to the cold glass. Far below, the train's lit windows slid across a frozen river like a row of gold stamps.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, chunky white plastic shell shaped like a small loaf of bread: about one and a half times as long front to back as it is tall, deep and boxy with softly rounded corners and a mostly flat top. It is not a round dome or ball, and not a long thin tube. It has an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck, about as tall as the head is long, made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. It has no arms and no hands. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: The duck stands alone in the aisle of a night train carriage between tall seats that rise above its head, a blank cardboard ticket tucked into its sweater collar, frosty fields in the dark windows. Panel 2: The duck braces its orange feet on the ribbed rubber floor as the carriage sways, treetops and telephone wires dropping away below the windows. Panel 3: The carriage tilts steeply uphill like a slide, and the duck leans its whole neck forward up the slope to stay standing. Panel 4: Two ducks: a second robot duck with no sweater, plain white and wearing a small conductor's cap, strolls easily down the slanted aisle toward the duck in the yellow sweater. Panel 5: Two ducks: the sweaterless conductor duck steps on a cardboard ticket lying on the floor, leaving an orange footprint on it, while the duck in the yellow sweater stands steady with its knees softly bent. Panel 6: The duck presses its camera eye to a cold train window on a long stone bridge, and far below a row of glowing gold train windows is reflected across a frozen river under a nearly full moon. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
